title: Getting Tier 1 Write
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien, a senior secondary humanities teacher in Australia, argues that schools chronically try to intervene their way out of problems that belong to first-tier instruction, and that writing instruction is the clearest example. His framing image is a slow puncture in a car tyre: pumping it up every morning works, but it never repairs the leak. Prompted by researchED sessions showing that teacher confidence in writing instruction is lowest in Years 11 and 12, he read three books (The Writing Revolution 2.0, The Writing Rope, Writing Fitness) and completed three AERO writing courses, and he reports the takeaways book by book and course by course. The through-line is that writing is cognitively demanding, genre-specific and does not develop by osmosis, so each subject teacher owns the writing of that subject rather than delegating it to the English department. He then describes three changes he has actually made: live modelling under a document camera with built-in opportunities to respond, explicit vocabulary and morphology teaching for terms like contractionary and cyclical, and the write-it-again-better elaboration routine. The piece doubles as a candid admission that his own schooling and teacher training taught him almost nothing technical about sentence structure or grammar. It closes by insisting that unless writing is embedded system-wide in tier 1 curriculum, progress will stay local and fragile.
points: The tyre-puncture analogy reframes intervention culture: tier 2 supports applied to a tier 1 instructional gap raise teacher workload exponentially without fixing the cause.

Data presented at researchED Canberra showed teacher confidence in writing instruction falling as students move up the years, with Year 11 and 12 teachers least confident, exactly where high-stakes written assessment concentrates.
Brien insists genre ownership sits with the subject teacher, since a persuasive English essay and a science practical report demand different tone, structure and nominalisation.

He swapped typed or animated model answers for a document camera so students watch writing being produced in the same format they must produce it, and inserted cold-call checkpoints to stop the I-do phase going passive.
Morphological breakdowns (con/tract/ion/ary, cycle/ic/al) are offered as a concrete way to convert vocabulary students can spell into vocabulary they can use correctly.
quotes: If you had a puncture in your car tyre which was leading to a slow leak of air throughout the day, you could intervene every morning by pumping the tyre full of air. It would be effective in the short term. It would work. What it doesn’t do, is solve the underlying problem. It is a tier 2 intervention attempting to solve a tier 1 problem.

Many schools however, attempt to tier 2 their way out of an inherent tier 1 problem. This creates a challenge where more students are requiring additional support in their learning which increases the teachers workload exponentially.

This writing instruction needs to become a part of the tier 1 instruction and curriculum of every subject area. Tier 1 is not just your domain specific knowledge. Tier 1 encompasses everything a student requires to be successful in the subject.

The key conceit put forward by Hochman and Wexler is that ‘Writing should be taught, not caught’. A simple statement to make and yet it says something incredibly powerful about the way writing is (or more likely isn’t) being taught in many secondary schools.

Even more challenging is that writing does not come naturally the way that speaking does. It needs to be explicitly taught and modelled and even knowing ‘how to write’ is not enough as the individual also requires an in depth knowledge of the subject they are writing about to write coherently about it.
What all of these approaches miss is that students do not see writing occur in a way that mimics how they are required to write.
The genre of the summative assessment means that the appropriate grammar and punctuation for that genre needs to be explicitly taught by that subjects teacher.

As Dylan Wiliam has said previously feedback should lead to an action. If we provide students with feedback on their writing but do not ask them to apply that feedback then they are likely to make that same mistake again in the future.
